text.en: Would you like to explore a forest, or hunt for a hidden treasure, or build a model? Your choices show what kind of adventurer you are. In this story by Ruskin Bond, a boy named Suraj has an adventure at a railway tunnel in the jungle, and meets a watchman with a most unusual friend.

A little quiz asks how you like to spend weekends, which places you prefer to explore, what activity you would do and how you feel about teamwork. Your answers suggest a type such as Bold Explorer, and you discuss it with classmates.
It is almost noon, the jungle is very still, and heat waves shimmer along the railway embankment. The two rails are like black serpents disappearing into the tunnel in the hill. Suraj has cycled out of town, taken the jungle path, left his cycle in a village and walked over a scrub-covered hill to wait near the cutting. He is not catching a train; he wants to watch the steam engine come roaring out of the tunnel. He hears a shrill whistle, then a sound like distant thunder, and the engine shoots out like a green, black and gold dragon, showering sparks and roaring a challenge to the jungle. Hot steam strikes his face, and even the trees seem to flinch. When the train has gone, smoke drifts over the shisham trees and the jungle is still. Suraj walks into the tunnel. It gets pitch dark after about twenty yards, and the far opening is just a small round circle of light. He looks back to reassure himself that there is daylight outside. He walks on only to find out what the inside of a tunnel is really like. The walls are damp and sticky, a bat flies past and a lizard scuttles between the rails.
Coming out into the glare, Suraj is dazzled. On the hillside he thinks he sees a flash of orange and gold and a long swishing tail between the trees. Near the tunnel is the watchman's hut, with marigolds in front and a vegetable patch behind. The watchman, Sunder Singh, walks through the tunnel every day before the train, and if something is wrong he walks up the line and waves a red flag, so that the driver slows down. At night he does the same with an oil lamp. He welcomes Suraj and teases him for inspecting his tunnel. He says it is his tunnel because no one else wants it, and he has only lent it to the Government. He tells Suraj that the animal he saw was a leopard, his leopard, which minds its own business and visits the range for a few days each month. He does not lend it to the Government. He invites Suraj to come and see the night mail, which comes at about nine, and promises to take him home afterwards. He says it is safer in the jungle than the town, where he was almost run over by a bus. Then he covers his face with a banana leaf for a nap, saying animals rest in the heat of the day, but boys will not.
The next evening at dusk, as flying foxes swoop out of the trees, Suraj goes to the hut. The air smells of mango blossoms and promises rain. Sunder Singh has watered his garden and makes tea, and they listen to the tailorbird and the seven sisters. When night falls, the forest comes alive with the call of a barking deer, the cry of a fox and the tonk-tonk of a nightjar, and creaks and whispers like trees stretching their limbs. Sunder Singh goes to inspect the tunnel with his lamp and hears a padded footfall and a rustle of dry leaves. Ten minutes before the night mail, a sawing sound comes from the tunnel, which he says is the leopard, probably inside the tunnel. If they do not drive it out, the train will run it over, and he cannot let that happen. Suraj, sharing his concern, insists on coming. Sunder Singh takes an axe, though he says the leopard knows him, has a weakness for goats and stray dogs and will not harm them. He walks in shouting, while Suraj, whose throat is dry, cannot shout. About twenty paces in, the lamplight falls on a lithe and sinewy leopard crouching between the tracks. It bares its teeth and snarls, but when both shout together, uncertain how many humans there are, it turns and disappears into the darkness. They walk the length of the tunnel to make sure it has gone. The rails begin to hum and tremble, and the train thunders past like the dragon of Suraj's dreams. Then silence returns and the forest seems to breathe again.
Almost a week later, Suraj and his father travel on the same night mail. His father is going to Delhi on business and has decided to take him along, to learn about his business. Suraj looks out of the window into the darkness and, as the engine whistles near the tunnel, he sees the lamp, though not Sunder Singh. He knows his friend is out there. He thinks of the watchman, who will always remain like a firefly for the travellers, lighting up the darkness for steam engines and leopards.
Suraj compares the train to a dragon, a beautiful monster out of his dreams. He knew the train was near because of a shrill whistle and a sound like distant thunder from the tunnel. Inside the tunnel Suraj saw damp, sticky walls, a bat and a lizard. Sunder Singh says the tunnel is his, but lent to the Government. The watchman's system is: before every train he inspects the tunnel; if all is well he returns to his hut and naps; if something is wrong he walks up the line and waves the red flag by day or the lamp at night, to warn the driver; and if all is well at night he hangs the lamp at his hut and sleeps. Sunder Singh knew the leopard was in the tunnel because he heard its footfall and a sawing sound. Suraj could not shout at first because he was afraid. The leopard disappeared because both of them shouted together. Suraj knew his friend was there because he saw the lamp. The story shows Suraj's curiosity and courage, Sunder Singh's kindness and sense of duty, and a gentle respect for wild animals. It is an adventure, with description of sights, sounds and smells that make the jungle come alive.
Words in the text include shimmered, shone with a light that seems to move; cutting, a narrow valley cut through a hill for a railway; instinctively, without thought; flinch, make a quick movement; plume, a long thin cloud; scuttled, ran hurriedly; dazzled, blinded by bright light; obstacles, things that block the way; lithe, thin and graceful; sinewy, lean and muscular; and defying, opposing. Figures of speech include the rails as two black serpents, a metaphor, and the train as a dragon, a comparison that shows how Suraj sees it. Describing the sounds of the forest uses imagery of sound, smell and sight.

text.en: Before each train.

why.en: He walks the length of the tunnel.

text.en: Warn the driver.

why.en: He waves a red flag by day or a lamp at night.

problem.en: Find a metaphor in the story.

text.en: Look for a thing called another thing.

why.en: The rails are two black serpents.

text.en: Check there is no like or as.

prompt.en: Tell what happens at the tunnel and what it shows about Suraj and Sunder Singh.

requiredIdeas.en: Suraj waits to see the steam train and walks into the tunnel.
He meets Sunder Singh, the watchman, and hears about his leopard.
Together they drive the leopard out so that the night train does not run it over.
Suraj later sees the watchman's lamp from the train.

commonMisconceptions.en: The watchman owns the whole railway.

points.en: The Tunnel is an adventure by Ruskin Bond set in a jungle railway cutting.
Suraj meets Sunder Singh, a watchman, who lends his tunnel to the Government and has a leopard friend.
They drive the leopard out of the tunnel before the night mail.
Suraj later recognises his friend's lamp from the train.
Imagery and metaphor, such as serpent rails and a dragon train, make the story vivid.
